correctness.rationale: The Brownian-bridge cross-covariance functions yield exact integrated gains \(J_m(t)/(\eta+V_m(t))\). Differentiating the position gain gives a factored numerator with positive decreasing \(A\) and increasing \(D\), establishing the unique position optimum and the exact endpoint threshold \(11/336\). The velocity gain has a one-crossing first-order condition with strictly increasing time-to-noise function. At both unique optima, observation variance satisfies \(V_{\mathrm p}\le1/12<6/25<V_{\mathrm v}\); differentiating the log ratio of optimal gains therefore proves there is exactly one mode crossing. Exact rational comparisons locate it strictly after the position endpoint threshold and before \(1/25\). Elimination yields the degree-seven polynomial, whose derivative is strictly negative throughout the bracket by seven exact Bernstein coefficients. A standalone script rederives all symbolic identities and rational comparisons, plus supplementary numerical covariance quadratures. The argument handles all \(\eta>0\) and both endpoints; numerical sampling is not substituted for proof.

originality.rationale: The claim is the unique all-noise optimum over a calibrated choice of one displacement or one derivative measurement of an integrated Brownian bridge, with an exact endpoint and mode-switch threshold. Lachal provides the integrated bridge object and covariance, Ji and Müller the general Gaussian trajectory-design criterion, and existing derivative-only timing does not compare the two modes. No inspected full text or indexed statement covers the global two-mode switch or implies its exact critical polynomial without the new comparison proof. Priority remains qualified by an unavailable dissertation full text and potentially unindexed equivalents.

value.rationale: With one measurement of an integrated random trajectory, choosing the observable (displacement versus derivative) is as important as choosing its time. The bridge is a natural finite-horizon stochastic benchmark. The proof supplies a complete all-noise decision rule, the sharp \(11/336\) terminal-position transition, a later unique seventh-degree modality switch, and a discontinuous move in optimal sampling time. These distinctions are not generic consequences of covariance positivity or a cheap normalization check; they quantify a meaningful resource-limited sensing decision and provide an exact benchmark for Gaussian design algorithms. Scope and model-dependent noise calibration are explicitly disclosed.
